3D Narrative Puzzle Adventure · Luski Game Studio · Released on Steam, Nov 2020

Owned the second act of an award-winning narrative puzzle game, from camera and controls to puzzle layouts, and the playtests that shaped it.

Recognition: Games for Change Latin America 2020 – Winner, Best Game for Social Impact · BIG Festival 2021 – Finalist, Impact category

Aurora is a short, emotional game about the impact of an environmental disaster, seen through a child's eyes. Players explore, solve environmental puzzles and follow the story across three acts, in about \[X\] hours. It was made for players of all ages, including people who rarely play games.

ASSET – 3–4 screenshots: one from each act, plus one Act II puzzle space. Wide shots that show the environment work best.

blocks.html:
1. Feel before challenge. Movement and camera have to feel right before any puzzle can be fair.
  2. Show, don't tell. The game teaches through space, motion and discovery, not text.
  3. Gentle mastery. Puzzles grow from intuition to insight, and failing never punishes the player.

[embedded content: design pillars · 3 pillars under one goal\]

In a narrative game, how it feels is the first impression. Before a puzzle can be fair or a story can land, players have to trust how the character moves and how the camera shows the space. I co-defined the 3C with the design team, and designed the camera and controls for Act II.

The camera's job is to reveal the puzzle, not fight it.

  • Framing that hints at the goal: default angles keep the next objective in view, so the space suggests where to go.
  • Smooth, predictable follow: no sudden snaps or fast rotation, to avoid motion sickness in players new to 3D.
  • Composed angles for story moments: fixed or guided shots where the story needs them.

ASSET – Camera comparison: two screenshots or short GIFs of the same space, showing the framing before and after a change. If no "before" exists, a top-down sketch of camera zones in one Act II area works well.

blocks.text: Character and control: forgiving by design

blocks.html:
For an all-ages audience, the controls have to turn what the player means into what the character does.

  • Generous tolerances: wider interaction ranges and forgiving collision, so near-misses count.
  • Gentle assists: \[for example: ledge help, coyote time, auto-alignment to interactable objects; confirm which existed\].
  • Readable animation: the character's pose shows clearly what state it's in and what it can do next.

The aim was that failing feels like learning, never like fighting the controls.

blocks.html: ASSET – Movement GIF: 5–10 seconds of the character moving through an Act II space, ideally including a near-miss the tolerances saved.

I owned the gameplay of the whole second act: its structure, its puzzles, and how each space teaches the player something new. I refined the blockouts with level design so the spaces guide players without hand-holding.

Act II alternates puzzle spaces with quiet moments for the story, so challenge never runs long enough to tire young players, and emotional beats land when the player has room to feel them.

ASSET – Beat chart (high value, easy to make): a simple line chart of Act II from start to end. X axis: the act's spaces or minutes. Y axis: intensity (challenge or emotion). Mark each puzzle, each story beat and each new mechanic. You can draw it from memory in a spreadsheet; recruiters love this kind of chart because it shows how you think about pacing.

Each mechanic follows the same four steps, so Act II needs no text tutorials:

  1. Introduce it in a safe space where failure costs nothing.
  2. Practise it in a simple puzzle with one clear solution.
  3. Combine it with a mechanic the player already knows.
  4. Master it in a puzzle that needs both, for an earned "aha".

blocks.text: Iteration case 1: the puzzle players couldn't see

blocks.html:
[embedded content: iteration case 1 · problem to result\]

Problem: in one Act II puzzle, testers kept missing a key interaction point. They got stuck, lost the story's momentum, and some left the session early.

Cause: the camera and sightlines pulled attention away from the object players needed, and nothing in the space pointed to it.

Options considered:

  • Add an on-screen prompt. Rejected: it breaks the no-text pillar and gives the answer away.
  • Make the object glow constantly. Rejected: it removes the discovery and looks out of place in the art style.
  • Change how the space presents it. Chosen: fix the problem where it started.

Fix: I reframed the camera to bring the objective into view, adjusted sightlines in the blockout with level design, and added lighting cues that lead the eye without spelling out the answer.

Result: about 90% of testers solved the puzzle in the following rounds \[from about X% before\], and the "aha" moment stayed intact.

ASSET – Before and after: two screenshots from the same camera position, before and after the change. This one image pair makes the whole case.

A second case makes the page much stronger, because it shows the first one wasn't luck. Some prompts to jog your memory: a control or camera problem young players had; a puzzle that was too easy or too long; a story moment testers missed; something you cut and why.

  • Problem: \[what testers did or said\]

  • Fix: \[what you changed\]
  • Result: \[what changed in the next test\]

• No text tutorials. Teaching through space took far more design and testing time than a prompt would have, but it kept the story wordless and the pillars intact.
  • Forgiving controls over precision. Generous tolerances meant puzzles could never rely on precise platforming; challenge had to come from understanding, not dexterity.

What worked

  • Teaching through space instead of text kept the story intact and worked for players of all ages.
  • Testing with first-time players early found problems the team could no longer see.

What I'd do differently

[Pick what's true; this section is a strong senior signal, because it shows you judge your own work.\]

  • Set measurable targets, such as solve rate and time per puzzle, before the first playtest rather than during.
  • Test the camera with first-time players earlier, since many later fixes were camera fixes.

What I learned

  • For young or new players, the camera does most of the teaching.
  • What seems obvious to a designer often isn't; test early with people who have never seen the game.
